summary: Specifies version 2 of the Network Time Protocol, which synchronizes clocks and distributes time across a large internet. It describes the formal structure and gives implementation information. It is historic and was replaced by RFC 1305.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1119 specifies NTP version 2, which lets time servers and clients synchronize clocks across a network. It describes message exchanges, server selection, clock adjustment, and optional authentication.

questions: how does ntp choose a time server
subtitle: A specification for synchronizing clocks across an internet of time servers and clients.

tldr.problem: Time servers and clients need to synchronize clocks despite variable network delays, unreliable paths, and possible failures.
tldr.mechanism: NTP version 2 arranges time servers and clients in a self-organizing hierarchy, exchanges timestamped messages, filters measurements, selects a clock source, and adjusts local clocks.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1119 is Historic and has been obsoleted by RFC 1305.

today: RFC 1119 is Historic and has been obsoleted by RFC 1305.

sections.title: A Hierarchy of Time Servers
sections.content:
NTP connects primary reference sources, such as radio clocks, to primary time servers. Secondary servers obtain time from primary or other secondary servers, and can distribute it to clients. A server's stratum indicates its level in this hierarchy: primary servers use stratum 1, and each level below has a stratum one greater than the preceding level.

The network can reorganize when servers or paths fail. The RFC describes selecting paths with a minimum-weight spanning tree and warns that the synchronization subnet must not form a loop.
sections.plainLanguage: Primary servers receive time from reference sources. Other servers get time through them, and clients can get time from those servers.

sections.title: Exchanges and Operating Modes
sections.content:
NTP supports five modes: symmetric active, symmetric passive, client, server, and broadcast. In client/server mode, a client sends periodic messages and the server replies; the server need not keep state between client requests. Symmetric modes let peers synchronize each other, while broadcast mode lets a server send periodic messages to peers.

The message includes timestamps for the request's departure, its arrival at the server, the reply's departure, and the reply's arrival at the client. These values allow the client to estimate clock offset and roundtrip delay.
sections.plainLanguage: Hosts can exchange time as peers, use a client-and-server arrangement, or receive broadcasts. The message timestamps help estimate both the time difference and network delay.

sections.title: Filtering Measurements and Choosing a Clock
sections.content:
NTP collects offset and delay samples from its peers. The clock-filter procedure selects the sample with the minimum delay and estimates the quality of the path from the samples.

The clock-selection procedure builds a set of candidate servers, orders them by estimated reliability and accuracy, and removes outliers. It selects a surviving candidate as the system's clock source, if one remains.
sections.plainLanguage: NTP compares repeated measurements and gives less weight to noisy data. It then selects a suitable server from the candidates that remain.

sections.title: Timestamps and Authentication
sections.content:
An NTP timestamp is a 64-bit unsigned fixed-point number representing seconds since 0 hours on 1 January 1900. Its first 32 bits are the integer part and its last 32 bits are the fractional part; the RFC gives its precision as about 200 picoseconds.

Authentication is optional. The RFC describes a message authenticator using a key identifier and crypto-checksum, but NTP itself does not distribute or manage the keys. The RFC says the authentication mechanism is not required for conformance.
sections.plainLanguage: The timestamp has one part for whole seconds and one for a fraction of a second. Optional authentication can check messages, but key distribution is outside the protocol.
